lead: Every diffusion calculation needs one number: the diffusivity D<sub>AB</sub>, the constant in Fick's law that says how quickly A spreads through B. You cannot read it from a table for every pair, so engineers either measure it in a small cell or predict it from simpler properties. Measurement gives the truth for one pair; prediction gives a quick estimate before a pilot plant exists. The same number sizes absorbers, dryers and membrane units. This chapter shows the standard methods for gases and liquids, the units each one uses, and the order of magnitude to expect.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.3 for Fick's laws and Chapter 1.4 for the flux equations used to interpret a measurement; the ideal gas law from Chapter 1.1.

sections.h3: What D is and how big it is

blocks.text: The diffusivity D<sub>AB</sub> is the proportionality constant in Fick's first law for A diffusing through B. Its SI unit is m²/s; older tables use cm²/s, and 1 cm²/s = 10⁻⁴ m²/s. For any binary pair D<sub>AB</sub> = D<sub>BA</sub>. Typical values near room temperature are 10⁻⁵ m²/s in gases, 10⁻⁹ m²/s in liquids and far less in solids; D rises with temperature and, in gases, falls with pressure.

The orders matter in design. A gas-phase value near 10⁻⁵ m²/s means a species crosses a millimetre in about a tenth of a second; a liquid-phase value near 10⁻⁹ m²/s takes about a thousand seconds for the same distance. That is why absorbers and extraction columns use stirring, packing or small droplets: the molecular value alone would need an impractically tall column. Flow adds eddy diffusion on top, as the mass transfer coefficient topic shows.

Two-bulb method for gases. Two bulbs of volume V each are joined by a tube of length L and cross-section S. One bulb starts rich in A, the other poor. With equal volumes and equimolar counter-diffusion, the mole-fraction difference Δy falls exponentially:

blocks.where: Δy₀ is the initial mole-fraction difference; Δy is the difference at time t; S is the tube cross-section in m²; L is the tube length in m; V is each bulb volume in m³; t is time in s.

blocks.text: A plot of ln(Δy₀/Δy) against t is a straight line through the origin, and D<sub>AB</sub> comes from its slope. Winkelmann's method uses the Stefan tube of the previous chapter. A volatile liquid sits in a narrow vertical tube at constant temperature; air sweeps the open top, so y<sub>A2</sub> = 0 there and y<sub>A1</sub> is the vapour-pressure value at the liquid surface. The level is read as the gas path grows from z₀ to z. The pseudo-steady result, rearranged, is a straight line:
t/(z − z₀) = [ρ<sub>L</sub> (y<sub>B</sub>)<sub>lm</sub> / (2 M D c y<sub>A1</sub>)] (z − z₀) + ρ<sub>L</sub> (y<sub>B</sub>)<sub>lm</sub> z₀ / (M D c y<sub>A1</sub>)
blocks.where: ρ<sub>L</sub> is the liquid density (kg/m³), M its molar mass (kg/mol), c = P/RT the gas concentration (mol/m³), (y<sub>B</sub>)<sub>lm</sub> the log-mean air fraction between the surface and the top. Plot t/(z − z₀) against (z − z₀): the slope s gives D = ρ<sub>L</sub> (y<sub>B</sub>)<sub>lm</sub>/(2 M c y<sub>A1</sub> s). The initial path z₀ need not be read exactly, which is why the method is popular.

blocks.text: For liquids the diaphragm cell is standard. Two stirred compartments are separated by a porous glass diaphragm. The cell constant β is found once by calibrating with a pair of known D, such as dilute KCl in water. Then ln(Δc₀/Δc) = β D<sub>AB</sub> t.

Kinetic theory gives the Chapman–Enskog equation, right to a few per cent for non-polar gases. It needs the Lennard–Jones collision diameter σ<sub>AB</sub> (in Å) and a collision integral Ω<sub>D</sub>, read from a table against k<sub>B</sub> T/ε<sub>AB</sub>:

blocks.where: D<sub>AB</sub> in cm²/s, T in K, P in atm, M in g/mol, σ<sub>AB</sub> in Å. Because σ and Ω<sub>D</sub> are not always at hand, most hand calculations use the Fuller–Schettler–Giddings correlation:

D<sub>AB</sub> in cm²/s; T in K; P in atm; M in g/mol; Σv<sub>A</sub> and Σv<sub>B</sub> are sums of tabulated diffusion-volume increments (not molar volumes). Take the cube root of each sum, add them and square the result.

blocks.text: Read the dependence, not just the formula. D rises as T<sup>1.75</sup> and falls as 1/P. Doubling pressure halves D at the same temperature. The correlation gives cm²/s only when P is in atm; if you feed kPa you get a value too small by the conversion factor. Convert to m²/s at the end by multiplying by 10⁻⁴.
Liquid diffusivities are harder because molecules touch. The Stokes–Einstein relation treats the solute as a sphere of radius r moving through a continuum of viscosity μ:

blocks.where: k<sub>B</sub> = 1.381×10⁻²³ J/K is the Boltzmann constant; T is absolute temperature in K; μ is viscosity in Pa·s; r is the solute radius in m; D<sub>AB</sub> is in m²/s.

blocks.text: The key scaling is D ∝ T/μ: warm a liquid and D rises; thicken it and D falls. The relation suits large spherical solutes, less so small molecules.

Wilke–Chang is the common engineering correlation for a dilute solute. It uses the solvent viscosity μ<sub>B</sub>, an association factor φ (2.6 for water, 1.9 for methanol, 1.5 for ethanol, 1.0 for non-polar solvents) and the solute molar volume at its normal boiling point V<sub>A</sub>, often from Le Bas increments:

blocks.where: D<sub>AB</sub> in cm²/s; T in K; μ<sub>B</sub> in cP; V<sub>A</sub> in cm³/mol; M<sub>B</sub> is the solvent molar mass in g/mol. A correct liquid answer lies near 10⁻⁵ cm²/s (10⁻⁹ m²/s); a value near 10⁻¹ cm²/s means a gas formula slipped in. The Hayduk–Laudie form for water drops φ.

examples.question: Estimate the diffusivity of CO2 in air at 300 K and 1 atm with the Fuller correlation. Data: M of CO2 = 44 g/mol, M of air = 29 g/mol, diffusion volume increments Σv = 26.9 for CO2 and 20.1 for air.
steps: Correlation with P in atm gives D in cm²/s: D<sub>AB</sub> = 1.00×10⁻³ T<sup>1.75</sup> (1/M<sub>A</sub> + 1/M<sub>B</sub>)<sup>0.5</sup> / [P (Σv<sub>A</sub><sup>1/3</sup> + Σv<sub>B</sub><sup>1/3</sup>)²].
examples.answer: D<sub>AB</sub> for CO2 in air at 300 K and 1 atm is about 0.158 cm²/s, that is 1.58×10⁻⁵ m²/s.
examples.check:
import math
T = 300.0
P = 1.0
M<sub>CO2</sub> = 44.0
M<sub>air</sub> = 29.0
Sv<sub>CO2</sub> = 26.9
Sv<sub>air</sub> = 20.1
mass_term = math.sqrt(1/M<sub>CO2</sub> + 1/M<sub>air</sub>)
D<sub>cm2</sub>_s = 1.00e-3 * T**1.75 * mass_term / (P * (Sv<sub>CO2</sub>**(1/3) + Sv<sub>air</sub>**(1/3))**2)
D<sub>m2</sub>_s = D<sub>cm2</sub>_s * 1e-4
print(f"{D<sub>cm2</sub>_s:.4f}")
print(f"{D<sub>m2</sub>_s:.3e}")

examples.question: Estimate the diffusivity of ethanol (A) at low concentration in water (B) at 298 K by Wilke–Chang. Water: μ<sub>B</sub> = 0.89 cP, M<sub>B</sub> = 18.02, φ = 2.6. Le Bas volumes: C 14.8, H 3.7, O (in an alcohol) 7.4 cm³/mol. The measured value is about 1.24×10⁻⁵ cm²/s.
steps: Molar volume of C₂H₅OH: V<sub>A</sub> = 2(14.8) + 6(3.7) + 7.4 = 59.2 cm³/mol, so V<sub>A</sub><sup>0.6</sup> = 11.57.
Compare: (1.47 − 1.24)/1.24 = 0.18, so the estimate is 18 % high, inside the usual 10 to 20 % band for this correlation.
examples.answer: D<sub>AB</sub> ≈ 1.47×10⁻⁹ m²/s, about 18 % above the measured 1.24×10⁻⁹ m²/s and four orders of magnitude below a gas diffusivity.

traps: Fuller's correlation wants P in atm and returns cm²/s. Put 101.3 kPa in place of 1 atm and your answer is about 101 times too small.
Σv is a diffusion volume increment from a table, not the molar volume. Do not use 22.4 L/mol.
D<sub>AB</sub> = D<sub>BA</sub> for a binary gas pair. Do not mix D (m²/s) with the mass transfer coefficient k<sub>c</sub> (m/s).
Stokes–Einstein says D ∝ T/μ, not μ/T. Check the direction: a thicker liquid slows diffusion.

quiz.q: Define diffusivity D<sub>AB</sub> and give its SI unit.
quiz.a: D<sub>AB</sub> is the proportionality constant in Fick's first law for A diffusing through B; it is the flux per unit concentration gradient. SI unit: m²/s.

quiz.q: Why is D<sub>AB</sub> = D<sub>BA</sub> for a binary mixture?
quiz.a: In a binary mixture J<sub>A</sub> = −J<sub>B</sub>, and because y<sub>A</sub> + y<sub>B</sub> = 1 the gradients satisfy dy<sub>A</sub>/dz = −dy<sub>B</sub>/dz. Writing Fick's law for each, −c D<sub>AB</sub> dy<sub>A</sub>/dz = +c D<sub>BA</sub> dy<sub>A</sub>/dz with a minus sign on J<sub>B</sub>, so the two constants must be equal: D<sub>AB</sub> = D<sub>BA</sub>. The argument needs only two species, not an ideal gas.

quiz.q: Use Fuller to estimate D for O2 in N2 at 350 K and 2 atm. Data: M<sub>O2</sub> = 32, M<sub>N2</sub> = 28, Σv O2 = 16.6, Σv N2 = 17.9.
A student measures D for CO2 in air with a two-bulb cell but forgets to thermostat; room temperature rises 5 K during the run. Will the reported D be too high or too low? Use T<sup>1.75</sup>.
quiz.a: D rises with T<sup>1.75</sup>, so the fitted slope is an average over a higher temperature. The reported D is too high compared with the value at the starting temperature; the run should be reported with its temperature range.

quiz.q: A liquid has viscosity 1.0 cP at 300 K. Estimate D for a solute of radius 0.5 nm using Stokes–Einstein. k<sub>B</sub> = 1.381×10⁻²³ J/K.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern laboratories measure D by Taylor dispersion and pulsed-field-gradient NMR, and process simulators fall back on group-contribution estimates when data are missing. Search for Taylor dispersion analysis and PFG-NMR diffusometry.
